title: The desire for God (CCC 27)
hookLine: the longing for God is written in every heart

lines: SHE GETS THE THING SHE WANTED.
CHAPTER ONE STARTS WITH THE ACHE.
cards: A woman gets the job she worked toward for years. The offer letter, the new desk, the dinner to celebrate. And it's good.
It really is. But a few weeks in, something small shows up, like hunger after a big meal: is this it? She wonders if she's ungrateful.
She wonders if something's broken in her. She doesn't tell anyone. The first chapter of the Catechism of the Catholic Church doesn't start with rules.
It starts with that ache. Today: desire.

teach.b: First, where it begins. Paragraph 27, the start of the Catechism's first chapter, says the desire for God is written in the human heart, because people are made by God and for God.
And it says God never stops drawing people toward himself. Only in God, it says, will a person find the truth and happiness they never stop looking for.
So, in the Catechism's view, that ache after the good thing isn't a defect. It's a signature. Second, the oldest voice.
A few paragraphs on, the Catechism quotes Augustine, from the opening of his Confessions, in a line addressed to God.

teach.h: RESTLESS UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.
teach.b: In Pusey's translation: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." You heard its echo in young Merton's restlessness. Here it becomes the foundation of the whole book.
Third, everywhere. The Catechism notes that, throughout history, people have searched for God in prayers, sacrifices, rituals and quiet meditation.

It calls the human being a religious being. It doesn't treat that search as a problem, but as a trace of the desire. It also admits honestly that people can forget this longing, or push it away, or never think about it.
Fourth, the psalm. Long before Augustine, a psalm put it in one picture, in the Douay-Rheims: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God."
A deer at a stream, thirsty.

teach.h: SO MY SOUL PANTETH AFTER THEE.
teach.b: Catholics say that thirst isn't the problem. It's the clue: a sign of being made for more.

how: The Catechism of the Catholic Church opens its account of the faith with the human desire for God (paragraphs 27–30), and quotes Augustine's line about the restless heart (paragraph 30).

o: a longing for God written into every heart
a craving for things you know are wrong
a wish for success, money and comfort

games.q: you have the career, the friends, the good life, and you're still restless. what does Augustine say that means?
o: you need a bigger version of the same things
your heart is restless until it rests in God
restlessness is a sin to be ashamed of
games.why: Augustine opens his Confessions saying we were made for God, and the heart is restless until it rests in him. the Catechism builds on it.

practice: Ask yourself honestly: what do I want?

Let the first answers come, money, rest, love, to be understood, without judging them; then ask underneath, and what do I want from that, gently, one layer at a time, until you reach something you can't quite name, and stay there.
If you pray, you can offer that longing to God, just as it is.

wordCard.voice: Desire, the ache for God the Catechism says is written into every human heart, the longing Augustine called restless until it rests in God. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: our heart is restless, from the first chapter of Augustine's Confessions.

carryVoice: Your line: made for more. The Catechism calls that ache a signature, not a defect. See you tomorrow.
